title: Photo-induced CO2 reduction by hydrogen for selective CO evolution in a dynamic monolith photoreactor loaded with Ag-modified TiO2 nanocatalyst
abstract: Ag-promoted TiO2 nanoparticles immobilized over the cordierite monolithic support for dynamic and selective photo-reduction of CO2 to CO by the use of hydrogen has been investigated. Ag-loaded TiO2 NPs synthesized by a facile sol–gel method were coated over the monolith channels by dip-coating method. The samples were characterized by XRD, Raman, FTIR, SEM, TEM, XPS, N2 adsorption–desorption, UV–Vis and PL spectroscopy. The photo-activity test of Ag-modified TiO2 NPs was conducted for dynamic photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2 as a reductant via a reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction in a cell type and monolith photo-reactors. Using 5 wt. % Ag/TO2 NPs, CO2 was energetically converted to CO with a yield rate 1335 μmole g-catal.−1 h−1, a 111 fold-higher than the amount of CO produced over the pure TiO2 catalyst. More importantly, photo-activity of Ag/TiO2 catalyst for CO evolution can be improved by 209 fold using monolith photo-reactor than the cell type reactor under the same operating conditions. This enactment was evidently due to the efficient light harvesting with larger illuminated surface area inside monolith micro-channels and efficient charges separation in the presence of Ag-metal. The reusability of Ag/TiO2 NPs loaded over the monolithic support showed favorable recycling capability than the catalyst dispersed in a cell reactor. A possible reaction mechanism for this observation has been discussed in detail.
paragraphs: Global warming effects due to rise in the atmospheric CO2 levels and energy shortages by the excessive usages of fossil fuels are the cause of great concerns. In addition of capture and sequestration, photocatalytic CO2 conversion to chemicals and fuels is considered as an innovative and environment-friendly approach. Thus, reutilization of CO2 would be helpful in alleviating global temperature and could offer an alternative pathway toward renewable fuel production. The photocatalytic reduction of CO2 by H2O to chemicals and fuels, in particular, CO has been reported by many researchers, since it can be converted to fuels through Fischer-Tropsch. However, one of the primary drawbacks in photo-catalysis is the lower yield and selectivity provided by the photo-catalysis system.

Among the semiconductors, a suitable photo-catalyst should be low-cost, nontoxic, chemically and thermally stable, available in excess and effective to utilize light irradiation. TiO2 is typically a good semiconductor choice because of obvious benefits and fulfills many of these criteria. However, its lower photo-activity is one of the prime drawbacks due to high electron–hole recombination rate and is active only under ultraviolet (UV) light irradiation owing to its wide band gap. Additionally, it has high recombination rate of photo-generated (e−/h+) charges and uncontrolled photo-reduction selectivity. To improve performances of photo-catalysts with effective charge carrier utilization, many strategies have been developed such as metals-loading, semiconductors coupling and co-catalysts modifications.

An attractive approach to decrease this effect is to improve electron transport in the system by modifying TiO2 structure with transition metal and/or noble metal ions. Noble-metals loaded onto TiO2 prevent recombination rate of photo-generated electron–hole pair's (e−/h+). During the last years noble metals such as Au, Ag, Pt and Cu have been investigated to give higher TiO2 photoactivity in CO2 photoreduction process. For example, Au-loaded TiO2 nanoparticles were investigated for selective photocatalytic CO2 conversion to CO. Cu/TiO2 catalyst found very efficient for selective production of CH4 in the photocatalytic CO2 reduction with water. The use of PtCu2OTiO2 co-catalysts significantly enhanced the reduction of CO2 to CH4 and Cu-loaded In2O3/TiO2 photo-catalysts promoted the conversion of CO2 to CH4 and CH3OH.

Recently, Ag loaded photo-catalysts have been reported to lead an enhancement in photocatalytic performance due to reduce in the charge carrier recombination rate. The modification of MWCNT/TiO2 by Ag for photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2O to CH4 and C2H4 was reported with enhanced photo-activity provided by Ag metal. Ag/Ga2O3 catalyst was tested for photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2O promoted by Ag clusters in Ag/Ga2O3 catalyst. Ag-loaded Ga2O3 with a ZnGa2O4 layers was tested for CO production during CO2 reduction with H2O with enhanced photo-activity and selectivity. Ag NPs modified TiO2 Nano-rods has been found very efficient for photo-reduction of CO2 to CH4 using H2O as a reductant. With plasmonic Ag-NPs deposited on carbon quantum dots/graphitic carbon nitride, a significantly enhanced photo-activity towards hydrogen production was reported by Qin et al.. Selective photocatalytic CO2 conversion to CO/CH4 was detected over Ag-loading on brookite TiO2 nano-cubes. Enhanced activity of Ag-loaded MgO/TiO2 catalyst was reported for photocatalytic conversion of CO2 with H2O to CH4. Similarly, Ag/ZnGa2O4 catalyst for CO2 reduction with H2O to CO and Ag@AgBr/CNTs for CO2 reduction with H2O to CO, CH4 and CH3OH have been investigated by various researchers. Evidently, Ag-metal plays the role of electrons trapper, preventing the recombination of electron–hole pair and consequently promoting photo-activity in photo-induced CO2 reduction applications.

In addition of efficient photo-catalysts, the reductant choice is of great importance, as it effects the overall CO2 reduction process efficiency and products selectivity. In order to achieve the reduction of CO2, H2O is usually fed as a reducing agent. Thermodynamically, photocatalytic conversion of CO2 with H2O over heterogeneous photo-catalysis is not a favorable process because reduction of H+, released from H2O, usually competes with CO2 reduction. This is because H2O reduction potential to generate H2 is lower (0 eV) than the CO2 standard reduction potential (−1.9 eV). Under such conditions, a reduction competition can be developed between CO2/H2O, thus photoreactions would be more favourable for conversion of H2O to produce H2 instead of CO2 reduction to CO. Recently, we investigated H2 as a potentially viable reductant for CO2 reduction to CO and CH4 over different type of photocatalysts. The performance of nano-catalysts was significantly enhanced when H2 was employed as a reducing agent compared to H2O for selective CO production. The hydrogen can be produced economically using photo-catalytic water splitting process under solar energy irradiations. Therefore, it is appropriate to investigate H2 as a reductant for photocatalytic CO2 to CO conversion via reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction using Ag-modified TiO2 nano-particles.

On the other hand, photo-catalysis process is considered efficient only if there is good interaction between the light irradiations, catalyst and reactants. To date, slurry and cell type photo-reactors have been widely explored in which catalysts are used as a suspension or distributed over the reactor surface. The slurry type reactors have limitations such as (1) poor light utilization efficiency due to less exposed active surface area, (2) the loss of catalyst during recycling, (3) high cost of photo-catalyst separation from the slurry system, and (4) lower intensity to stimulate complex nature of photocatalytic reaction. Therefore, the design of highly efficient photo-reactors for CO2 reduction is crucial to scale up photo-technology from the laboratory to commercial level.

During the recent years, immobilized photocatalytic systems with enhanced light utilization efficiency have attracted much attentions. Among the different supports, monolithic substrates are mainly studied because of their unique structure and large photonic efficiency. Lately, monolithic support found very efficient for photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO with enhanced selectivity and yield. To the best of our knowledge, based on available data, the application of Ag-NPs-promoted TiO2 supported over monolithic structure for the conversion of CO2 to CO with H2 as a reducing agent via RWGS reaction has never been reported.

The objective of this study was to investigate the performance of Ag-modified TiO2 catalysts immobilized onto cordierite monolithic support for dynamic and selective CO2 reduction with hydrogen via RWGS shift reaction. The performance of photo-catalysts were further compared in a cell type and monolith photo-reactors. The quantum efficiency was calculated to compare the performances of both the catalysts and reactors with the reported values. The catalyst stability was critically evaluated to deliberate the reusability in cyclic runs. A possible reaction mechanism for the improved photocatalytic performance was proposed.

All reagents were of analytical grade and used without further purification. The silver modified TiO2 nanoparticles were synthesized by a facile sol–gel method and were coated over monolithic support reported in our previous work. Typically, 10 mL titanium tetra isopropoxide and 7.5 mL 1 M acetic acid solution were added into a 30 mL isopropanol under vigorous stirring. The mixed solution was kept stirring for 24 h at an ambient temperature. Later, calculated amount (wt. %) of silver nitrate (AgNO3 3H2O) dissolved in isopropanol was added to titanium suspension and stirred for another 6 h until a thick sol obtained. The sol-obtained was coated over monolith channels using dip-coating method.

The cordierite monoliths were supplied by Pingxiang Meitao Chemical Packing Co., Ltd. China. The dimensions of monolith used were diameter 6 cm; length 2 cm and channels per square inch (CPSI) 200. Initially, monoliths were washed with acetone and ethanol to remove any organic materials, then dried at 110 °C overnight under airflow. The initial weight of cleaned and dried monoliths were calculated. For every sample, three readings were noted for the bare as well as the coated monoliths and their average values are reported. For catalyst coating, weighed monoliths were dipped in the resulting Ag-loaded TiO2 sol for 10 s and excessive sol was blown off with hot compressed air. The coating procedure was repeated to the desired catalyst loading over the monolith channels. The catalyst loaded monoliths were dried at 100 °C overnight, calcined at a rate of 5 °C min−1 up to 500 °C, and then held for 5 h. Finally, the actual amount of catalyst loaded was calculated by subtracting the final weight of coated monoliths from the initial weight of un-coated monolith. The obtained samples were denoted as Ag-loaded TiO2 nanoparticles immobilized over monolithic support. Different levels of Ag loading into TiO2 e.g., 3, 5 and 7 wt. % were obtained by varying the quantity of silver nitrate adding into titanium sol. Besides, pure TiO2 NPs and powder Ag-loaded TiO2 NPs were synthesized using the similar procedure as mentioned above.

X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) was obtained on Bruker D8 advance diffractometer. CuKα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm) operating at 40 kV and 40 mA. A scan range of 10 ≤ 2θ ≤ 80°, a scan speed of 1.2° per min and a step size of 0.02°. Raman measurements of the powder samples were acquired at room temperature using Raman Spectrometer (LabRAM HR Evolution, HORIBA) with a 532 nm emitting laser as an excitation source. The cordierite structure of monolith was investigated with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) carried out with JEOL JSM6390 LV SEM instrument. The morphology of the materials was examined using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) using Hitachi SU8020 instrument with double condenser optics to ensure full control of probe current from 1 pA to more than 5 nA. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) was conducted for both the fresh and used samples. The BET specific surface area and pore size of the samples were analyzed using N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms with Micrometrics ASAP 2020 operated at 77 K. All the samples were degasified at 250 °C for 4 h under vacuum. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed using Omicron DAR 400 analyser. The samples were fixed to the sample holder using carbon tape. The peaks were calibrated at 284.60 eV as an internal carbon standard. UV–Vis diffuse reflectance absorbance spectra (DRS) of the samples were determined using Agilent, Cary 100 UV–Vis spectrophotometer equipped with an integrated sphere. Initially, blank runs were conducted to correct the base line. The absorbance spectra were analysed at ambient temperature in the wavelength range of 200–800 nm. The photoluminescence (PL) spectra were measured using photoluminescence PerkinElmer LS-55 Luminescence Spectrometer at excitation wavelength 350 nm. Fourier Transformed Infrared (FT-IR) Spectrometer peaks of the fresh and used catalysts were obtained in the range of 400–4000 cm−1 employing Spectrum 2000 Explorer Spectrometer.

The activity of photo-induced CO2-hydrogen reaction system was tested in a gas phase photo-reactor with H2 as a reducing agent under UV-light irradiation as depicted in Fig. 1 . The reactor consists of cylindrical stainless steel vessel with a total volume of 150 cm3, equipped with a quartz window for passing light irradiations from the reflector lamp at the top. The light source used was a 200 W Hg lamp with light intensity 150 mW cm−2 at wavelength 252 nm. The light intensity was measured with an online optical process monitor ILT OPM-1D and a SED008/W sensor. The cooling fans were installed at the top and sides of the lamp for continuous removal of lamp heat. The reactor was covered with aluminum foil to ensure lights for reactions came through the quartz window only. The gasses feed rates were controlled using online mass flow controllers (MFC) with gas flow measurements in the range of 10–500 mL/min. A gas mixture was used to ensure all the gases were uniformly mixed before entering into reactor. The temperature of the reactor was controlled using temperature controller while pressure was measured using pressure gauge.

In case of the cell type photo-reactor, 25 mg of catalyst powder was suspended uniformly inside the reactor at the bottom surface to ensure efficient light distribution over the entire catalyst surface as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a). The schematics of monolith photo-reactor for CO2-hydrogen reaction system is portrayed in Fig. 1 (b). The monolithic supports have cordierite honeycomb structure and were purchased from Pingxiang Meitao Company, China. All the monoliths were cylindrical in shape, having dimensions of 60 mm in diameter and 20 mm in length. The catalyst coated ceramic monoliths with channel per square inch (CPSI) 200 were inserted inside the stainless steel chamber. After performing a leak test with helium (He) at 2 bars pressure, the reactor was purged using helium (He) flow before gas mixtures (CO2 and H2, purity = 99.99%) was continuously passed through the reactor at a flow rate of 20 mL per minute. All the experiments were carried out in a continuous mode of operation. The CO2/H2 feed ratio 1.0 was fixed and flow rates of 20 mL/min were adjusted with a space velocity of 0.13 s−1. All the experiments were conducted at 100 °C and atmospheric pressure.

The gas products were analyzed using an on-line gas chromatograph (GC-Agilent Technologies 6890 N, USA) equipped with thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionized detector (FID). Furthermore, FID detector was connected with a HP-PLOT Q capillary column (Agilent, length 30 m. ID 0.53 mm, film 40 μm) for separation of C1 C6 paraffin and olefins hydrocarbons, alcohols and oxygenated compounds. The TCD detector was connected to UCW982, DC-200, Porapak Q and Mol Sieve 13X columns. C1 C2, C3 C5 compounds and light gasses (H2, O2, N2, CO) were separated using Porapak Q, DC-200 and MS-13X column, respectively.

The XRD spectra of TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples are presented in Fig. 2 (a). In the bare TiO2 sample, the characteristic peaks identified were 25.61° (101), 38.15° (004), 48.32° (200), 54.10° (105), 55.35° (211), 62.92° (204), 69.10° (116), 70.57° (220) and 75.40° (215), corresponds to anatase phase of TiO2. The XRD peaks of Ag-loaded TiO2 also reveal a pure crystalline and anatase phase TiO2. The peaks pertaining to rutile phase of TiO2 were not detected in both the pure TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples. Similarly, Ag-modified TiO2 samples show broad and intense signals, yet peaks pertaining to Ag in metal or oxide states were not detected. This was perhaps the amounts of Ag-loaded in the TiO2 was below the detection limit of the instrument or due to highly dispersed Ag-NPs inside TiO2 structure. The crystallite size was calculated using Scherrer equation based on the XRD (101) peak. In the case of Ag-loading, the crystallite size gradually decreased, possibly Ag hindered TiO2 crystal growth. Ag-loading gave a gradual reduced crystallite size of the TiO2 samples as summarized in Table 1 . Additional information regarding the phase of the nanomaterials was obtained by Raman spectroscopy.

The phase identification of the TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples was further investigated using Raman spectroscopy performed in the range of 100–1000 cm−1 and the results are shown in Fig. 2 (b). In the pure anatase TiO2, the intense Raman signal with Eg (1) mode appeared at 142 cm−1 followed by less intense signals with modes Eg (2) and Eg (3) were observed at 197 cm−1 and 634 cm−1, respectively. Similarly, B1g peak appeared at 394 cm−1 and mode (A1g + B1g) detected as a single merged peak at 513 cm−1. All these peaks reveal the characteristics of the pure anatase phase of TiO2. The Raman spectra of Ag/TiO2 samples are identical to that of the pure TiO2, which clearly indicated that the TiO2 retained its structure after Ag loading. No signals relating to Ag in Ag/TiO2 sample were identified because of the relatively low concentration of Ag loaded into TiO2 and due to its weak Raman scattering. However, changes were obvious in the position with broadened peaks. With Ag-loading, the Raman band Eg (1) was shifted towards higher wavenumber while band B1g and Eg (3) broadened. Similar observation have been reported previously. These observations can confirm successful loading of Ag NPs over the TiO2 surface without any phase change.

The morphology of cordierite support and catalyst particles was investigated by SEM as demonstrated in Fig. 3 . The bare monolithic channels of cordierite structure is obvious in Fig. 3 (a). Fig. 3 (b) depicts the surface of bare monolith channel, yet nanoparticles were not detected. In Fig. 3 (c), it can be apparently seen that catalyst was deposited evenly over the cordierite surface with no broken layer. The sol–gel dip-coating method used to support catalyst inside the channels resulted in a good dispersion of catalysts over the cordierite surface. The FESEM image of mesoporous structure of Ag/TiO2 NPs over the channels surface could be seen in Fig. 3 (d).

The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 sample are shown in Fig. 4 . The TEM images of low and high magnification in Fig. 4 (a and b) show mesoporous structure of Ag-loaded TiO2 nanoparticles. It is obvious, TiO2 NPs were spherical in shape with agglomerates due to hindered crystal growth by the presence of Ag. The dark spots reveal the existence of Ag-NPs on the TiO2 surface. The HR-TEM image of Ag/TiO2 NPs in Fig. 4 (c) shows lattice fringe with d-spacing value of 0.35 nm, which corresponds to (101) plane of the anatase phase of TiO2. Fig. 4 (d) depicts the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns of Ag/TiO2 NPs. The pattern clearly reveals bright concentric rings, which were due to the diffractions from the anatase phase TiO2.

The N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms and corresponding pore size distribution curves of TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples are depicted in Fig. 5 . All the isotherms in Fig. 5 (a) show a type IV with high volume of N2 adsorption in a high relative pressure (P/Po) region. It can also be observed that the size of hysteresis loop between adsorption and desorption branches is larger in high level of Ag-loading TiO2 samples. The initial part of the isotherms at relatively low pressure (low P/Po) reveals monolayer-multilayer adsorption on the internal surface of the pores. This is also associated with fluid to crystalline phase transition of the adsorbed N2. However, capillary condensation could be seen in the upper part of isotherms when moving along the curve toward high relative pressure (high P/Po) part, where the steep increment in the adsorption volume can be observed. This phenomenon of adsorption can only happen when the pores become saturated with the liquid N2. The pore size distribution curves of TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 nanoparticles in Fig. 5 (b), present two different two pore size distribution from 3 to 14 nm and 2–6 nm for TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples, respectively.

The BET specific surface areas, pore volumes and pore sizes of TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 samples are tabulated in Table 1. The measurement shows that BET surface area (SBET) of pure TiO2 was 43 m2/g, increased to 50 and 63 m2/g in 3 and 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 samples, respectively. The Ag-loaded TiO2 samples have larger pore volume than the bare TiO2, attributed to improve in the meso-porosity of TiO2. Similarly, BJH pore diameter was gradually decreased in Ag-loading TiO2 samples. The increase in BET surface area and pore volume with reduced pore diameter may be resulted from the hindered crustal growth of TiO2 with improved meso-porosity by Ag-loading.

The chemical state of elements in Ag-loaded TiO2 sample with binding energies was investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) as shown in Fig. 6 . The Ti 2p spectrum in Fig. 6 (a) shows the peaks with binding energies (BE) positioned at ∼ 458.23 eV (2p3/2) and 463.91 eV (2p1/2), attributed to Ti4+ oxidation state or TiO2. In the XPS spectrum of Ag in Fig. 6 (b), showing two individual peaks positioned at 367.57 and 373.60 eV with 6.0 splitting between two peaks corresponds to Ag 3d5/2 and 3d3/2 and demonstrated as Ag0 or metallic silver. The spectrum of O 1s in Fig. 6 (c) reveals peaks centered at 529.47, 531.52 and 533.32 eV. The BE value of 529.47 eV is attributed to the lattice oxygen O2− in TiO2, which is in agreement with the reported values. The oxygen peaks at around 531.52 eV and 533.32 eV are due to H2O or the free hydroxyl group (OH) to the surface. Furthermore, Fig. 6 (d) shows the presence of two peaks of C1s located at 284.60 eV and 288.37 eV. The high resolution peak at 284.6 eV is ascribed to elemental carbon CC in the sample, while the one at 288.37 eV corresponds to CO. The presence of elemental carbon may be recognized as the carbon from carbon tap used for analysis of sample.

The optical properties of the samples were measured using UV–Vis DRS in the wavelength range of 200–800 nm. Fig. 7 (a) depicts UV Vis diffuse reflectance spectra of TiO2 and Ag-modified TiO2 samples. Compared to pure TiO2, all the Ag/TiO2 samples presented the increase in the optical absorbance. An estimate of the optical band gap (Eg) of the Ag/TiO2 samples has been obtained using the Kubelka–Munk function F(R). The band gap energies were determined from the plot of (FR × hv)1/2 versus photon energy (hv) by extrapolating the linear region of the plot to the intercept of the photon energy axis as shown in Fig. 7 (b). The calculated band energy values of TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 catalysts are listed in Table 1. The band gap energy of the pure TiO2 was 3.11 eV, reduced to 3.01 and 2.97 eV for 3 and 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 samples, respectively. This reiterates Ag impurity level is beneficial in extending the absorption spectrum wavelength towards the visible region.

The hindered, transfer and recombination process of photo-generated charges in the photo-catalyst samples were analysed by PL as displayed in Fig. 8 . The emission peaks of all the samples were in the range of 450–550 nm when samples were excited at wavelength of 350 nm. In both the TiO2 and Ag-modified TiO2 samples, emitted peaks exhibited strong PL signals in the identified regions. Compare with the TiO2, the emission peak intensity of Ag-loaded TiO2 samples gradually decreased. The existence of PL emission is attributed to the recombination of free charge carries (e−/h+). The weaker intensity of Ag/TiO2 samples indicates a lower recombination possibilities of electron–hole (e−/h+) pairs on the surface of TiO2. Therefore, addition of Ag into TiO2 catalyst would be more capable to reduce charges recombination rate to enhance TiO2 photo-activity for CO2 reduction applications.

The TiO2 and Ag/TiO2 samples were analysed for the reduction of CO2 to CO in the presence of H2 as a reducing agent under UV light irradiation in a continuous flow cell type and monolith photo-reactor. The blank tests were conducted to confirm all the products were originated from CO2 reduction only.

Fig. 9 shows the results of dynamic CO, CH4 and hydrations production as a function of irradiation time over the pure TiO2 and Ag-loaded (Ag = 3, 5 and 7 wt. %) TiO2 samples at feed flow 20 mL/min and CO2/H2 feed ratio 1.0. Fig. 9 (a) relates, for the bare TiO2, limited photo-activity registered and giving rise to small amounts of CO evolution, attributed to higher electron–hole pair's recombination rate. Photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO gradually increased over the irradiation time, and then reached to steady state. When the TiO2 samples containing Ag were employed, a substantial increase in CO2 reduction to CO was detected. This considerably improved TiO2 photo-activity in the presence of Ag was obviously due to the charge separation and transport by Ag. In addition, the higher surface area provided by the monolithic support favoured a homogenous distribution of the Ag nanoparticles resulting in more light harvesting. Addition of more amounts of Ag, more CO was produced, whereas, 5 wt. % Ag-loading was the optimum, then the yield rate gradually decreased with Ag-loading. At excess amount of Ag-loading, lower CO yield can be attributed to the formation of charge recombination centers over the TiO2 surface.

Fig. 9 (b) shows the yield of CH4 evolution during photo-induced CO2 reduction with H2 using monolith photo-reactor and feed flow rate 20 mL/min with CO2/H2 molar feed ratio 1.0 at different irradiations. Noticeably, the CH4 production trends are entirely different than CO over the irradiation time irrespective the type of photo-catalysts used. Initially, a significant increase in CH4 production was detected, then decreased rapidly at an elongated reaction time. However, a gradual increase in the production of CH4 could be seen by loading more Ag-contents into TiO2. In this respect, Ag/TiO2 co-catalyst efficiently contributes to conduct electrons towards CO2, thereby converting CO to CH4. The declined in CH4 yield over the irradiation time can be explained based on the oxidation of CH4 with O2 to CO2, probably due to very efficient photocatalytic reaction in the presence of monolithic catalysts. However, amount of O2 produced was not detected during CO2 reduction process due to limitations of GC configuration.

The production of hydrocarbons over Ag/TiO2 catalysts at different Ag-loading levels and irradiation times as shown in Fig. 9 (c). Initially, large amount of hydrocarbons were detected which were declined over the irradiation time and trends were consists in all photo-catalysts. Additionally, it could be seen that hydrocarbons production rate is higher in larger Ag-loading levels and the results are consistent with the CH4 production. However, the decrease in yield of hydrocarbons over the irradiation time was possibly due to their oxidation in the presence of O2. The hydrocarbons were not observed in the pure TiO2 catalyst, obviously due to lower its lower photo-activity. Among the hydrocarbons, C2H6 and C3H6 were produced in large amounts in the presence of TiO2 catalyst loaded with 7% Ag. These results have confirmed Ag as an efficient metal to improve TiO2 photo-activity for the reduction of CO2 via RWGS reaction in a monolith photo-reactor.

Fig. 10 shows the yield rate and selectivity towards CO formation for the photocatalytic conversion of CO2 by H2 over TiO2 and Ag-modified TiO2 photo-catalysts with various amounts of Ag-loading. All photo-catalysts tested could reduce CO2 for dynamic CO evolution as the main product under UV-light irradiation. With the Ag-loading, the selectivity towards CO formation approached to 99.8%, implying that RWGS reaction preceded efficiently over Ag-loaded TiO2 catalysts. Similar observations have been reported during CO2 reduction to CO over Ag-loaded Ga2O3 catalyst. The summary of yield rates and selectivity of CO2 reduction products over TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 photo-catalysts has been presented in Table 2 . The maximum amount of CO detected over the optimal 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst supported over cordierite monolith was 1335 μmole g-catal.−1 h−1, a 111 fold more than the amount of CO produced over the pure TiO2 catalyst. The photo-catalysts activity for CO2 reduction to CH4 was in the order of 7% AgTiO2 > 5%Ag/TiO2 > 3%Ag/TiO2 > TiO2. Similarly, the yield of hydrocarbons production was higher in order of 7% AgTiO2 > 5%Ag/TiO2 > 3%Ag/TiO2. The selectivity of CO production was significantly higher in both TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 catalysts. The selectivity toward CO production over TiO2 catalysts was 96.31%, increased to 99.92% in 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 samples. As the selectivity of CO is greater than 99.9%, the photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2 through RWGS reaction is preferable in a continuous operation of monolith photo-reactor. The significantly enhanced photo-activity of Ag/TiO2 catalyst for dynamic and selective CO2 to CO conversion in a monolith photo-reactor was due to efficient adsorption–desorption processes with more production and separation of electron–hole (e−/h+) pairs inside monolith micro-channels.

Thermodynamically, photo-excited electrons with in the photo-catalyst could only be consumed effectively if the reduction potential of metal (Mn+) is more positive than the conductance band potential of the semiconductor (TiO2 = −0.5 V). The redox potential values of Ag+ and Ag2+ are given in Eqs (1) and (2). Evidently, silver has much lower redox value (more positive) than the CB of TiO2, thus silver could perform as an efficient source of sink to trap electrons. Therefore, significantly enhanced photo-activity of Ag/TiO2 catalyst was perhaps due to rapid transfer of excited electrons to the Ag-particles which could enhance the photocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction. (1) A g + + e − → A g E 0 = 0.79 V (2) A g 2 + + e − → A g + E 0 = 1.98 V

The performance of continuous monolith photo-reactor is further evaluated based on quantum efficiency (QE). The QE can be calculated as the ratio of production rate (mole per sec) of products with photonic flux (mole per sec) strikes over the catalyst surface. For the conversion of CO2 to CO, two electrons would be consumed and if one electron–hole pair is to be generated by one photon activation, then the quantum efficiency for CO production can be defined by Eq. (3). (3) QE ( % ) = 2 ×moles of CO production rate ( mol/sec ) moles of photon flux ( mol/sec ) × 100

Using bare TiO2, QE of 0.0013% was achieved for CO production which was augmented to 0.143% TiO2 sample loaded with 5 wt. % Ag. It is evident that QE for CO production was much higher in the presence of Ag-metal evidently due to hindered charge recombination rate and more light harvesting efficiency by monolith photo-reactor.

The performance of Ag-loaded TiO2 nano-catalyst was further investigated using cell type and monolith photo-reactors operating in a continuous mode of operation at feed flow rate 20 mL min−1, CO2/H2 feed ratio 1.0 and operating temperature 100 °C. The yield of CO production in a cell type and monolith photo-reactor over the irradiation time is presented in Fig. 11 (a). The amounts of CO produced using Ag/TiO2 NPs supported over monolith photo-reactor was 1335 μmole g-catal.−1 h−1, a 209 folds more than the CO produced in a cell type photo-reactor in which catalyst was dispersed over reactor surface. This significantly enhanced photo-activity of Ag/TiO2 catalyst in a monolith photo-reactor was evidently due to larger illuminated surface area with efficient utilization of light irradiations and more dynamic adsorption–desorption of species over the catalyst surface.

The production of CH4 in a cell type and monolith photo-reactor over Ag/TiO2 catalyst at different irradiation time is depicted in Fig. 11 (b). Initially, yield rate of CH4 production in a cell type and monolith photo-reactors were similar. However, over the irradiation time, production of CH4 in a cell type reactor declined rapidly, yet there was continuous production of CH4 in a monolith photo-reactor. These observations could be explained based on the adsorption–desorption process over the catalyst surface and reaction mechanism of CO and CH4 production as explained in mechanism section. In general, using cell type photo-reactor, desorption of reactants were not very fast, CO adsorbed over the catalyst surface was finally converted to CH4. However, in a monolith photo-reactor, these processes were very fast, thus only small amount of CH4 detected over the irradiation time. Similar observations has been reported previously.

It is generally accepted that the photo-catalyst efficiency is mainly dependent on the light absorption ability, surface properties (e.g., specific surface area, pore structure, pore volume and adsorption property etc.) and photo-generated electron/hole pairs separation efficiency. It is evidenced that photo-activity for CO evolution rate over the TiO2 can be improved by 111 fold via 5 wt. % Ag-loading. However, as discussed above that the TiO2 surface area is only slightly different than the Ag/TiO2 sample, indicating that this factor is not crucial to the photocatalytic activity for Ag/TiO2 in photo-catalysis application. Similarly, photo-activity for CO evolution rate over the 5 wt. %Ag/TiO2 can be improved by 209 fold more using monolith photo-reactor than the cell type reactor under the same operating conditions. Therefore, the enhanced photocatalytic activity of semiconductor photo-catalyst is greatly dependent on the type of photo-reactor used for activity test. The significantly enhanced CO yield inside monolith was evidently due to large illuminated active surface area inside micro-channels with efficient adsorption–desorption process. Therefore, the role of cordierite honeycomb monolith loaded with Ag is obvious for dynamic CO production in continuous photo-reactor operation.

The stability of Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst was further investigated to evaluate the life of catalyst in a continuous operation of monolith photo-reactor. In order to investigate the stability of Ag/TiO2 catalyst, all the experiments were repeated in cyclic runs under the identical operating conditions. After each cyclic run, the reactor was flushed with helium for 2 h before starting the next run. The reused stability analysis for photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2 to CO over 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst is illustrated in Fig. 12 (a). It is noticeable to see that CO production rate was higher in the first run which slightly decreased in the second and third experimental runs over the entire irradiation time. Therefore, the Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst immobilized onto monolithic support provides prolong stability in cyclic runs. The stability of Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst for photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH4 is presented in Fig. 12 (b). Compared to the first cyclic run, in the second cyclic run, the CH4 production increased significantly at the start of the run and then gradually decreased. This was perhaps due to some of the carbon species adsorbed over catalyst the surface was converted to CH4 as similarly reported previously. However, a decrease in activity observed in the third cyclic runs, possibly because the catalyst lost its partial photo-activity for CH4 production. The colour of Ag-loaded catalyst during photocatalytic CO2 reduction was only slightly changed in every cyclic run. These results confirmed higher stability of Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst supported over cordierite monoliths.

During the cyclic experiments, the color of the catalyst was gradually changed and deactivation was observed. Therefore, characterizations for the fresh and used catalyst was conducted to investigate about the deactivation perspective and change of morphology. The used sample was 5 wt. % Ag/TiO2 catalyst collected after 32 h reaction time in a third cyclic run. The coke formation on the surface of catalyst was investigated using Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) as depicted in Fig. 13 . Fig. 13 (a) and (b) depicts the morphology and composition of the fresh 5 wt. % Ag/TiO2 catalyst sample. It is obvious from the EDX analysis that Ag of 4.3 wt. % and carbon of 4.1 wt. % was present in the sample. The Ag-loading was much closer to the actual loading of 5 wt. % Ag, yet carbon was detected possibly due to organic species or due to carbon tape used for the sample analysis. On the other hand, carbon deposited on the surface of TiO2 was increased to 10.6 wt. % for catalyst used for 32 h in a continuous operation of monolith photo-reactor. This increased in the amount of carbon maybe due to adsorption of intermediate carbon species over the TiO2 surface during photo-induced CO2 reduction reaction. Therefore, partial loss of photo-activity was due to formation of carbon species over the Ag/TiO2 catalyst during photo-induced CO2 reduction with hydrogen in a dynamic monolith photo-reactor.

To further evaluate the carbon species deposited over the catalyst surface, FTIR analysis of 5 wt. % Ag/TiO2 catalyst before the reaction and after the third cyclic run was conducted and the results are depicted in Fig. 14 . The spectrum reordered for fresh Ag/TiO2 catalyst reveals absorption peaks at 1623 cm−1 and 3364 cm−1, and the broad absorption bands at 400-700 cm−1, which are attributed of the vibration of OH and TiO bonds. On the other hand, FTIR was employed to catalyst used for 32 h in cyclic runs to examine the presence of carbon and other intermediate species deposited over the Ag/TiO2 surface. Compared to fresh catalyst, the peak intensity detected at 1623 cm −1 was increased due to water produced during RWGS reaction which was adsorbed over the TiO2 surface. However, the peaks to classify coke were not identified in the pure and used Ag/TiO2 samples. Additionally, several peaks observed in the region of 950 cm−1 to 1400 cm−1 attributed to CO and intermediate hydrocarbons species adsorbed over the catalyst surface. The peak detected at 2919 cm−1 can be attributed to stretching vibration of CH group over the TiO2 surface. Therefore, the partial decreased in Ag/TiO2 photo-activity in cyclic runs was due to adsorption of intermediate carbon species over the catalyst surface which prevented dynamic photo-induced CO2 reduction to CO in a monolith photoreactor.

The reaction mechanism was studied to get insight of CO2 photo-reduction over Ag/TiO2 catalysts. In the photocatalytic CO2 reduction process, the mechanism for CO and hydrocarbon production is complex and begins upon the photo-excitation of semiconductor. The photo-generated electron (e−) and hole (h+) involves in breaking OCO and HH bonds with the formation of CO and CH bonds. The electron–hole pairs separation and production of CO and hydrocarbons are illustrated in Eqs. (4–10) (4) TiO 2 → h v e c b − + h v b + (5) Ag 2 + + e c b − → Ag (6) CO 2 + 2 H + + 2 e − → CO + H 2 O (7) CO 2 + 8 H + + 8 e − → CH 4 + 2 H 2 O (8) 2 CO 2 + 12 H + + 12 e − → C 2 H 4 + 4 H 2 O (9) 2 CO 2 + 14 H + + 12 e − → C 2 H 6 + 4 H 2 O (10) 3 CO 2 + 18 H + + 18 e − → C 3 H 6 + 6 H 2 O

As the photocatalytic activity is closely related to the band structure of photo-catalyst, separation and transportation of photo-generated carriers (i.e., electrons and holes) as well as the redox potential, the enhanced photocatalytic mechanism can be explained by the scheme presented in Fig. 15. These products can be understood by comparing the conduction and valance band bands energies of TiO2 with the reduction potential of CO2 for the production of CO, CH4 and hydrocarbons. Since, the conductance band of TiO2 (−0.50 eV) lies above the reduction potential of CO2/CO (−0.48 eV), CO production as the main product is possible. Under the light irradiations, VB electrons of TiO2 excited to CB creating holes in VB. Without metal-loading, these charges recombine back and only a fraction of electrons and holes participate in reduction and oxidation process, thus, TiO2 shows a quite low photocatalytic activity. When Ag was loaded on TiO2 surface, the CB electron of TiO2 can transfer to it which causes electron–hole pair separation. Furthermore, more electrons could be trapped if the metal reduction potential is more positive than the CB of TiO2. As the redox value of Ag+/Ag is lower (+0.79) than the CB of TiO2 (−0.50 V), thus electron can effectively be transferred to silver. This process eventually decreases the rate of recombination of the photo-generated electron–hole pairs. The monolithic support is well known in efficient light harvesting with excellent distribution over the catalyst surface. Thus, faster electron production over the Ag/TiO2 loaded monolithic surface and transfer to CO2 is expected to occur. The expressively enhanced in CO yield rate over Ag/TiO2 was clearly due to higher trapping and mobility of electrons by Ag for CO2 reduction inside monolith channels. In general, dynamic and selective CO2 conversion to CO at a higher yield rate was due to using cordierite honeycomb monolith support loaded with Ag/TiO2 nanoparticles.

Ag-loaded TiO2 nano-catalysts with different concentration of Ag were prepared via a modified sol–gel method and were immobilized over the monolithic support. The photo-activity test of Ag/TiO2 catalyst for dynamic CO2 reduction to CO with hydrogen via RWGS reaction was tested in a continuous cell type and monolith photo-reactor. CO2 was efficiently converted to CO as the main product over Ag/TiO2 in a monolith photo-reactor than using cell type photo-reactor. The maximum yield rate of CO over 5 wt. % Ag-loaded TiO2 was 1335 μmole g-catal.−1 h−1 at selectivity 99.92%, 111 times higher than the pure TiO2 catalyst using monolith photo-reactor. The enhancement in the photocatalytic activity of CO production was attributed to hinder charges recombination by Ag. Similarly, photo-activity for CO evolution rate over the 5 wt. %Ag/TiO2 can be improved by 209 fold more using monolith photo-reactor than the cell type reactor under the same operating conditions. The yield of CO was greatly augmented in the continuous monolith photo-reactor due to larger illuminated surface area, higher photon energy consumption and better reactor volume utilization. The stability test revealed the prolonged activity of the Ag-loaded TiO2 catalyst supported over monolith channels than using cell type photo-reactor. Therefore, cordierite monolithic support could improve photo-activity, selectivity and stability of photo-catalysts and it is appropriate for efficient photocatalytic CO2 reduction via RWGS reaction for CO production with enhanced yield rate and selectivity.
